questions.title: Hinge joint identification: the ankle
questions.question: Which of the following is a hinge joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket synovial joint, allowing movement in many directions, not the single-plane motion of a hinge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The wrist is an ellipsoid (condyloid) joint, which permits flexion, extension, abduction and adduction, more than a hinge allows.
explanations.C: Correct. The ankle is a synovial hinge joint formed between the tibia, fibula and talus, and like every hinge joint it moves around a single axis. That axis allows only dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, while side-to-side stability is provided by the medial deltoid ligament and the lateral ligament bands rather than by any bony freedom of movement. This restriction to one plane of motion is exactly what defines a hinge joint, and is why the ankle — unlike the ball-and-socket shoulder or the ellipsoid wrist — cannot abduct or rotate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The interosseous membrane is a fibrous joint (a syndesmosis), not a synovial hinge, and permits no independent movement of its own.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A suture is an immobile fibrous joint between skull bones, the opposite of a freely moving hinge.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ankle as a hinge joint permitting only dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

questions.title: Hinge joint identification: the elbow
questions.question: Which one of the following is considered a hinge joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A suture is an immobile fibrous joint, not a synovial hinge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is a fibrous syndesmosis joining the shafts of two bones, not a synovial hinge.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The wrist is an ellipsoid joint, permitting movement around two axes rather than the single axis of a hinge.
explanations.D: Correct. The elbow is classified as a synovial hinge joint, formed mainly between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna, with the radial head contributing a separate small articulation. As a uniaxial hinge it permits flexion and extension only, and cannot perform abduction, adduction or independent rotation at the joint itself. This single-axis behaviour is the defining feature shared by every hinge joint, whether at the elbow, the ankle or the interphalangeal joints of the fingers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The shoulder is a synovial ball-and-socket joint, the most mobile joint in the body, not a hinge.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the elbow as a hinge joint permitting flexion and extension only.

questions.title: Fibrous joint identification: sutures
questions.question: Which of the following joints is fibrous?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ball-and-socket is a synovial joint type, freely movable, not fibrous.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The elbow is a synovial hinge joint, not a fibrous one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The shoulder is a synovial ball-and-socket joint.
explanations.D: Correct. A fibrous joint unites two bones with fibrous tissue and allows no real movement, and sutures are one of its three named types, alongside gomphosis and syndesmosis. In a suture, the bones of the skull are held together by a thin sutural ligament, which is why the skull functions as a single rigid case despite being built from several separate bones. Sutures are also unusual among fibrous joints in that this ligament is gradually obliterated with age, unlike the periodontal ligament of a gomphosis or the interosseous ligament of a syndesmosis, both of which persist throughout life.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The intertarsal joints of the foot are synovial plane joints, allowing gliding movement.

questions.learning_objective: Identify sutures as one of the three named types of fibrous joint.

questions.title: What sutures are, beyond "fibrous"
questions.question: Sutures are best described as joints that…

options.E: present between the root of a tooth and its socket

explanations.A: Correct. A suture is one of the three named types of fibrous joint, and it is specifically the type that unites the bones of the skull with a thin sutural ligament sandwiched between them. Because that ligament is rigid and only very slightly compressible, sutures allow essentially no movement, which suits their role of holding the cranial vault together as a single protective case around the brain. This same sutural ligament is gradually obliterated with age, a fact that distinguishes sutures from the other two fibrous joint types, whose connecting ligaments persist for life.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The opposite is true: the sutural ligament of a suture is progressively obliterated (ossifies) with advancing age.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sutures are fibrous joints, united by a ligament, not by cartilage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sutures permit essentially no movement; they are immobile fibrous joints, not freely mobile synovial ones.
explanations.E: Incorrect. That description fits a gomphosis, a different named type of fibrous joint, not a suture.

questions.learning_objective: State that sutures unite skull bones by a sutural ligament that is obliterated with age.

questions.title: Gomphosis classification
questions.question: Gomphosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gomphosis is not united by cartilage; it belongs to the fibrous joint group.
explanations.B: Correct. Gomphosis is one of the three named types of fibrous joint, alongside suture and syndesmosis, and it describes a tooth root held in its bony socket by the periodontal ligament. Like every fibrous joint it allows no significant movement, its connecting tissue being a short, taut ligament rather than cartilage or a synovial cavity. This makes gomphosis the joint type examiners most often use to test whether a student can tell fibrous-joint subtypes apart, since a tooth-in-socket is such a distinctive, easily pictured example.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diarthrosis is another name for a freely movable synovial joint, which a gomphosis, with essentially no movement, is not.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synovial joint has a joint cavity and synovial fluid; a gomphosis has neither.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Polyaxial" describes a synovial joint moving around several axes, such as the shoulder, not a fibrous joint like gomphosis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gomphosis as a fibrous joint, a tooth root held in its socket by the periodontal ligament.

questions.title: Syndesmosis: the inferior tibiofibular joint
questions.question: The type of the inferior tibiofibular joint is…

explanations.A: Incorrect. A pivot joint is synovial and uniaxial for rotation, such as the superior radio-ulnar joint; the inferior tibiofibular joint is not synovial.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gomphosis describes a tooth held in its socket, not the union between the lower ends of the tibia and fibula.
explanations.C: Correct. The inferior tibiofibular joint is the classic example of a syndesmosis, the fibrous joint type in which two bones are held together by an interosseous ligament rather than by a joint cavity. This ligament allows the small amount of give needed for the fibula to accommodate the talus during ankle movement while still holding the two bones firmly apposed. Syndesmosis is one of the three named fibrous joint types, distinguished from a suture (a sutural ligament between skull bones) and a gomphosis (a periodontal ligament holding a tooth) by its interosseous ligament and its typical site between the shafts of two long bones.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sutures unite the bones of the skull, not the tibia and fibula.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The inferior tibiofibular joint has no cartilage plate between the bones; it is a fibrous, not a cartilaginous, joint.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the inferior tibiofibular joint as a syndesmosis, held by an interosseous ligament.

questions.title: Secondary cartilaginous joint: symphysis pubis
questions.question: Secondary cartilaginous joints……………….

options.B: Have a wide range of movement
options.D: Have the symphysis pubis as an example

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the primary cartilaginous joint, such as the epiphyseal plate, that ossifies as growth completes; a secondary cartilaginous joint is permanent and does not ossify.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A secondary cartilaginous joint allows only slight movement, far less than a synovial joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secondary cartilaginous joints are formed of fibrocartilage; hyaline cartilage is the tissue of a primary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.D: Correct. A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) unites two bones by fibrocartilage, lies in the midline, is permanent throughout life, and permits only a slight amount of movement, and the pubic symphysis is the standard example examiners quote. This is in contrast to a primary cartilaginous joint, which is hyaline, usually temporary, and ossifies once growth is complete. The intervertebral discs are the other commonly tested example of a secondary cartilaginous joint, sharing the same fibrocartilage, midline position and lifelong permanence as the pubic symphysis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Both quoted examples, the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral discs, belong to the axial skeleton, not the appendicular skeleton.

questions.learning_objective: State that a secondary cartilaginous joint is fibrocartilaginous, midline and permanent, exemplified by the pubic symphysis.

questions.title: Secondary cartilaginous joint: intervertebral disc
questions.question: Which one of the following is considered a secondary cartilaginous joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A suture is a fibrous joint, not a cartilaginous one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The interosseous membrane is also a fibrous joint, a syndesmosis, not cartilaginous.
explanations.C: Correct. The intervertebral disc is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), uniting adjacent vertebral bodies by fibrocartilage in the midline and permitting only a small amount of movement between any one pair of vertebrae. Although each individual disc allows only slight bending, the many discs of the vertebral column add together to give the spine as a whole a considerable range of flexion, extension and lateral bending. The pubic symphysis is the other standard example of this same joint type, sharing the fibrocartilage, midline position and lifelong permanence that define a secondary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The elbow is a synovial hinge joint, freely movable, not cartilaginous.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The shoulder is a synovial ball-and-socket joint, not cartilaginous.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the intervertebral disc as a secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.title: Synovial joints and free movement
questions.question: Synovial joints allow…….movement between their bony elements.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A joint that allows no movement at all is fibrous or a primary cartilaginous joint, not synovial.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Limited movement describes a secondary cartilaginous joint such as the pubic symphysis, not a synovial joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gliding is only one of the several movements a synovial joint can perform, not a description of how much movement it allows overall.
explanations.D: Correct. A synovial joint is the freely mobile joint type, found mostly in the limbs, and its wide range of movement is made possible by a fibrous capsule enclosing a joint cavity, hyaline articular cartilage over the bone ends, and a synovial membrane that secretes lubricating synovial fluid into that cavity. This combination of a lubricated, largely frictionless cavity and smooth cartilage-covered surfaces is what lets synovial joints move so much more freely than a fibrous or cartilaginous joint ever could. The exact type of free movement — hinge, pivot, gliding or multi-axial — then depends on the shape of that particular joint's articular surfaces.

questions.learning_objective: State that synovial joints are the freely mobile joint type.

questions.title: Synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid
questions.question: The part of the synovial joint responsible for secretion of the synovial fluid is the…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fibrous capsule encloses and strengthens the joint, but it is the membrane lining its inner surface, not the capsule itself, that secretes fluid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ligaments inside the capsule add stability to the joint; they play no part in fluid secretion.
explanations.C: Correct. The synovial membrane is a thin, moist, glistening layer lining the inside of the fibrous capsule and covering every internal surface of the joint except the articular cartilage itself, and it is this membrane that both secretes and reabsorbs the synovial fluid within the joint cavity. That fluid is pale yellow and viscous, much like egg albumin, and it lubricates and nourishes the avascular articular cartilage covering the bone ends. Without a functioning synovial membrane the joint cavity would have no lubricating fluid at all, and the cartilage surfaces would grind against one another with far more friction and wear.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyaline articular cartilage covers the bone ends and is lubricated by the fluid, but it does not secrete that fluid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A meniscus is an intra-articular fibrocartilage that deepens certain joint surfaces, such as in the knee; it has no secretory function.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the synovial membrane as the structure that secretes synovial fluid.

questions.title: Joint shape classification: the knee is condylar
questions.question: What type of joint is the knee, according to the shape of the articulating bones?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plane joint has flat surfaces that glide over each other, such as the intertarsal joints, not the curved surfaces of the knee.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ball-and-socket describes the shoulder or hip, where a rounded head sits in a cup-shaped socket; the knee's surfaces are not shaped this way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A saddle joint, such as the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, has reciprocally concave-convex surfaces on both bones, which is not how the knee's condyles articulate.
explanations.D: Correct. By the shape of its articulating surfaces the knee is classified as a condylar (bicondylar) synovial joint, in which the rounded femoral condyles articulate with the flatter tibial condyles. This shape gives the knee mainly a hinge-like flexion and extension, with a small amount of added rotation once the knee is flexed, which is why some texts also describe it loosely as a modified hinge. The presence of two separate condylar articulations, medial and lateral, each with its own meniscus deepening the tibial surface, is what distinguishes a condylar joint from a simple uniaxial hinge such as the elbow.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A pure hinge joint, such as the elbow, moves in one plane only; the knee's condylar surfaces permit the additional small rotation that a simple hinge does not.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the knee as a condylar joint by the shape of its articulating surfaces.

questions.title: Pivot joint: superior radioulnar
questions.question: What is the type of the superior radioulnar joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A hinge joint, such as the elbow, moves in one plane only; the radio-ulnar joints instead allow rotation.
explanations.B: Correct. The superior radio-ulnar joint is a synovial pivot joint, in which the head of the radius rotates within a ring formed by the radial notch of the ulna and the annular ligament. A pivot joint is uniaxial, permitting rotation around a single long axis and nothing else, and at this joint that rotation is what produces pronation and supination of the forearm together with its partner, the inferior radio-ulnar joint. The two radio-ulnar pivot joints working together are what let the hand turn palm-up or palm-down without any true movement occurring at the wrist itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by an interosseous ligament, such as the inferior tibiofibular joint; the superior radio-ulnar joint is synovial.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior radio-ulnar joint has a true joint cavity and synovial fluid, so it is synovial, not cartilaginous.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ball-and-socket describes a multiaxial joint like the shoulder; the superior radio-ulnar joint permits rotation about one axis only.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the superior radio-ulnar joint as a synovial pivot joint producing pronation and supination.

questions.title: Pivot joint: inferior radioulnar
questions.question: What is the type of the inferior radioulnar joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ball-and-socket describes a multiaxial joint such as the shoulder, not the uniaxial rotation of the inferior radio-ulnar joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior radio-ulnar joint has a synovial cavity, so it is a synovial joint, not a cartilaginous one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A hinge joint permits flexion and extension in one plane; the inferior radio-ulnar joint instead permits rotation.
explanations.D: Correct. Like its partner at the elbow end of the forearm, the inferior radio-ulnar joint is a synovial pivot joint, where the head of the ulna rotates against the ulnar notch of the radius. Acting together, the superior and inferior radio-ulnar joints allow the radius to rotate around the relatively fixed ulna, producing pronation and supination of the hand. Because a pivot joint is uniaxial, this pair of joints permits rotation only, with no independent flexion, extension, abduction or adduction of its own.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by an interosseous ligament with no true joint cavity, unlike the synovial inferior radio-ulnar joint.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the inferior radio-ulnar joint as a synovial pivot joint, paired with the superior joint for pronation/supination.

questions.title: Saddle joint: carpometacarpal joint of the thumb
questions.question: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is classified as which type of synovial joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb has a true synovial cavity, so it is not a fibrous joint at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A pivot joint permits rotation about one axis only, such as the radio-ulnar joints; the thumb's carpometacarpal joint moves quite differently.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This joint has a synovial cavity and fluid, so it is classified as synovial, not cartilaginous.
explanations.D: Correct. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the classic example of a synovial saddle joint, where each bone's articular surface is concave in one direction and convex in the other, fitting together like a rider on a saddle. This shape gives the joint biaxial movement — flexion/extension and abduction/adduction — and combining these also produces circumduction, together giving the thumb its wide range of motion and its ability to oppose the other fingers. This is considerably more freedom than a uniaxial hinge or pivot joint allows, which is exactly why the thumb can move so much more independently than the fingers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A hinge joint is uniaxial, permitting flexion and extension only; the saddle-shaped thumb carpometacarpal joint additionally allows abduction and adduction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb as a biaxial synovial saddle joint.

questions.title: Ellipsoid joint: the wrist
questions.question: Which one of the following is considered an ellipsoid joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A suture is an immobile fibrous joint, not a freely moving ellipsoid one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The interosseous membrane is a fibrous syndesmosis, not a synovial ellipsoid joint.
explanations.C: Correct. The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is the standard example of a synovial ellipsoid joint (also called condyloid), where an oval convex surface fits into a matching oval concave surface. This shape makes the wrist biaxial, permitting flexion, extension, abduction and adduction, and combining these four movements also produces circumduction. Unlike a hinge joint such as the elbow, which moves in one plane only, an ellipsoid joint like the wrist cannot achieve full axial rotation, but it gains the abduction and adduction that a pure hinge lacks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The elbow is a hinge joint, uniaxial, permitting flexion and extension only.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, multiaxial rather than the biaxial ellipsoid wrist.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the wrist as a biaxial ellipsoid (condyloid) synovial joint.

questions.title: Shoulder dislocation vignette: ball-and-socket joint
questions.question: A young man was brought to the emergency room after a motorcycle accident. He complained of severe pain and was unable to move his right arm. Radiological examination revealed dislocation of the upper part of the humerus. What is the type of the joint involved?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A syndesmosis such as the inferior tibiofibular joint is fibrous and barely mobile; it is not the kind of joint that dislocates after trauma to the arm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A secondary cartilaginous joint, like the pubic symphysis, has no joint cavity and cannot dislocate in this way.
explanations.C: Correct. The joint dislocated here is the shoulder (glenohumeral) joint, a synovial ball-and-socket joint between the rounded head of the humerus and the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula. Its wide range of multiaxial movement is exactly what makes it the body's most mobile joint, but that same shallow socket and lax capsule that allow so much movement also make it the joint most commonly dislocated by trauma, as in this motorcycle accident. A ball-and-socket joint like the shoulder or hip is multiaxial, permitting flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction, in contrast to the single-plane movement of a hinge or the rotation-only movement of a pivot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A hinge joint such as the elbow moves in one plane only, quite unlike the multiaxial shoulder this vignette describes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A plane joint allows only small gliding movements between flat surfaces, not the wide range of motion and instability that make the shoulder prone to dislocation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the shoulder as a multiaxial synovial ball-and-socket joint prone to dislocation.

questions.title: Biaxial joint: the wrist
questions.question: One of the following joints is biaxial...

explanations.A: Incorrect. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, which is multiaxial (triaxial), not biaxial.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Like the shoulder, the hip is a ball-and-socket joint and therefore multiaxial rather than biaxial.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The elbow is a hinge joint, which is uniaxial, permitting flexion and extension only.
explanations.D: Correct. The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is an ellipsoid joint, and an ellipsoid joint is biaxial — it moves around two perpendicular axes, giving flexion/extension around one axis and abduction/adduction around the other, with circumduction as their combination. This is in contrast to a uniaxial joint such as a hinge or pivot, which permits movement around only one axis, and to a multiaxial (triaxial) joint such as the shoulder or hip, which moves freely around three. Recognising the wrist as biaxial, rather than uniaxial like the elbow or multiaxial like the shoulder, is what lets a student predict correctly which movements it can and cannot perform.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superior radio-ulnar joint is a pivot joint, which is uniaxial, permitting rotation only.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the wrist as biaxial, in contrast to uniaxial hinge/pivot joints and multiaxial ball-and-socket joints.

questions.title: Complex joint: the knee
questions.question: An example of a complex joint is the …

explanations.A: Incorrect. The wrist involves several carpal bones articulating with the radius, making it a compound rather than a complex joint, since it has no intra-articular disc comparable to the knee's menisci.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The elbow is formed by three bones (humerus, radius and ulna) meeting at one joint, making it compound, but it has no intra-articular meniscus, so it is not classified as complex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hip is a simple joint, formed by only two bones, the femur and the hip bone, with no intra-articular disc.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ankle is a compound joint, formed by the tibia, fibula and talus, but like the elbow it has no intra-articular meniscus and so is not complex.
explanations.E: Correct. Joints can be classified by the number of bones taking part: a simple joint has two articulating bones, a compound joint has more than two, and a complex joint additionally contains an intra-articular disc or meniscus dividing the joint cavity. The knee is the standard example of a complex joint, because in addition to the femur and tibia (with the patella articulating separately), it contains the medial and lateral menisci, fibrocartilaginous discs that deepen the tibial surfaces and cushion the joint. This third criterion — the presence of an intra-articular disc or meniscus — is what separates a complex joint from a merely compound one, which has extra bones but no such disc.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the knee as a complex joint, distinguished from a compound joint by its menisci.

questions.title: Basic definition of a joint
questions.question: The joint can be defined as:

options.B: Where two bones meet and move
options.C: The outer coating of the bone
options.D: The hard part of a skeleton
options.E: A simple connection between bone and muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect. A cushion-like structure, such as a meniscus or intervertebral disc, is a component found within some joints, not a definition of a joint itself.
explanations.B: Correct. A joint, or articulation, is defined as the point of union between two or more bones (or between bone and cartilage), and it is this union that permits or restricts the movement possible between them. This single definition covers every joint in the body, from an immobile skull suture to a freely moving shoulder, because what varies between joint types is not whether a union exists but how much movement that particular union allows. Classifying a joint as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial, and further by its shape or the number of bones and axes involved, is really just describing how that basic union between bones is built and how much motion it permits.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The outer coating of a bone is its periosteum, a completely different structure from a joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hard, rigid parts of the skeleton are the bones themselves; a joint is specifically the union between them, not the bone tissue.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A bone-to-muscle connection is a tendon's job, not a joint, which by definition unites two bones (or bone and cartilage), not a bone and a muscle.

questions.learning_objective: Define a joint as the point of union between two or more bones, permitting or restricting movement.

questions.title: Roof of the yolk sac: hypoblast
questions.question: The roof of the yolk sac is formed by…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiblast forms the floor of the amniotic cavity, on the opposite side of the bilaminar disc from the yolk sac.
explanations.B: Correct. On about the eighth day of development, the cells of the embryoblast facing the blastocele become cuboidal and form the hypoblast, and it is this hypoblast layer that lines the primary yolk sac, by way of Heuser's membrane, and later contributes to the definitive yolk sac as well. Because the hypoblast sits just beneath the epiblast and above the developing yolk sac cavity, describing it as forming the "roof" of the yolk sac captures its position relative to that cavity. The epiblast, by contrast, forms the floor of the amniotic cavity that opens above it, so the two layers of the bilaminar disc each face a different fluid-filled space.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer, invasive layer of the trophoblast that erodes the endometrium during implantation; it takes no part in forming the yolk sac.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cytotrophoblast is the inner, cellular layer of the trophoblast, a precursor of chorionic villi, not a contributor to the yolk sac wall.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The embryoblast (inner cell mass) gives rise to the epiblast and hypoblast in the first place; by the time the yolk sac forms it has already differentiated into those two layers.

questions.title: Implantation requirements: zona pellucida is not one of them
questions.question: All of the following structures are necessary for blastocyst implantation EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is required — the endometrium must be in its secretory (progestational) phase, thickened and receptive, for implantation to succeed.
explanations.B: Correct. By the time the blastocyst is ready to implant, it has already shed its zona pellucida — a process sometimes called hatching — so an intact zona pellucida is not present at implantation and is not one of its requirements. What implantation does require is a receptive, progestational (secretory-phase) endometrium, and a trophoblast that has already differentiated into its two layers, the inner cytotrophoblast and the outer syncytiotrophoblast, which does the actual invading. The zona pellucida's real job is earlier in development, blocking polyspermy at fertilisation and holding the dividing blastomeres together through cleavage, a role that is finished well before the blastocyst reaches the uterine wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is required — it is the syncytiotrophoblast that produces the enzymes eroding the endometrium and opening the implantation site.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is required — the cytotrophoblast is the inner trophoblast layer from which the invasive syncytiotrophoblast is generated.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This is required — implantation occurs within the functional layer of the endometrium, the same layer that is later shed as the decidua.

questions.title: Amniotic cavity forms between trophoblast and epiblast
questions.question: The amniotic cavity appears between the trophoblast and the...

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extraembryonic mesoderm does not appear until several days later, around day 11-12, well after the amniotic cavity has already formed.
explanations.B: Correct. The amniotic cavity opens within the inner cell mass on about the eighth day, appearing between the cytotrophoblast on one side and the epiblast on the other. Its roof is formed by a layer of flat cells called the amnioblast, derived from the trophoblast side, while its floor is formed by the tall columnar cells of the epiblast itself. This positions the new cavity directly against the epiblast, which is why the epiblast is described as facing, and forming the floor of, the amniotic cavity from the moment it appears.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane lines the primary yolk sac, on the opposite side of the bilaminar disc from the amniotic cavity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The connecting stalk links the embryo to the developing placenta and forms later; it is not one of the two structures bounding the amniotic cavity at its first appearance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The chorion is the outer, trophoblast-derived membrane of the whole gestational sac, a much larger and later structure than the thin amnioblast roof of the amniotic cavity.

questions.title: Definition of implantation
questions.question: What is implantation?

options.C: Embedding of the blastula in the endometrium
options.D: Removal of the seminal plasma proteins from the head of the sperm

explanations.A: Incorrect. That description is fertilisation, an event that happens in the uterine tube days before implantation, not implantation itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Repeated division of the zygote is cleavage, which produces the morula and then the blastocyst well before implantation occurs.
explanations.C: Correct. Implantation is the process by which the blastocyst becomes embedded within the superficial, functional layer of the endometrium, beginning with adhesion of its embryonic pole around the seventh day after fertilisation. It proceeds as the trophoblast differentiates into an inner cytotrophoblast and an outer, invasive syncytiotrophoblast, which erodes the endometrial epithelium and stroma so that the blastocyst can sink beneath the surface. By about the eleventh or twelfth day the surface epithelium has closed back over the breach, completing implantation and marking the point from which the other events of the second week — the bilaminar disc, the amniotic cavity and the primary yolk sac — all follow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Removal of the seminal plasma proteins from the sperm head is capacitation, which prepares the sperm to fertilise the oocyte, unrelated to the later embedding of the blastocyst.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The morula is the solid ball of cells produced by cleavage around day three or four, a stage that precedes both the blastocyst and implantation.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Define implantation as the embedding of the blastocyst within the endometrium.

questions.title: Normal implantation site: the endometrium
questions.question: Where does normal implantation occur?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Implantation in the uterine (fallopian) tube is the commonest form of ectopic, not normal, pregnancy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ovarian implantation is a rare form of ectopic pregnancy, not the normal site.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vagina plays no part in implantation; it is the birth canal, well below the site where the blastocyst embeds.
explanations.D: Correct. Normal implantation takes place within the endometrium, the mucosal lining of the uterine cavity, specifically in its superficial functional layer, which is receptive to the blastocyst during the secretory phase of the cycle. This is what distinguishes a normal, intrauterine pregnancy from an ectopic pregnancy, in which the blastocyst implants somewhere else along its journey, most often within the uterine tube. The endometrium's glandular secretions and thickened, vascular stroma at this phase of the cycle are exactly what make it, and not the deeper myometrium or any site outside the uterus, the normal home for implantation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The myometrium is the muscular wall of the uterus, deep to the endometrium; normal implantation stays within the endometrium and does not reach the muscle layer.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: State that normal implantation occurs within the endometrium, distinguishing it from ectopic sites.

questions.title: Normal implantation site: posterior wall near the fundus
questions.question: What is the normal site of implantation, more precisely, within the endometrium?

options.D: Posterior wall of the endometrium near the fundus of the uterus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Placenta previa is an abnormal, low implantation near the internal os, not the normal fundal/posterior site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tubal pregnancy is the commonest form of ectopic implantation, occurring in the uterine tube rather than the uterus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ovarian pregnancy is a rare ectopic implantation on the ovary itself, not the normal intrauterine site.
explanations.D: Correct. Within the endometrium, the normal site of implantation is more precisely the upper part of the posterior wall of the uterine body, close to the fundus, with the upper anterior wall as a less common alternative. Implanting here places the developing placenta well away from the internal os of the cervix, leaving the lower uterine segment and cervical canal clear for delivery later in pregnancy. Each of the other listed options names an abnormal site instead: placenta previa is implantation low in the uterus near the os, and tubal, ovarian and peritoneal pregnancy are all forms of ectopic implantation outside the uterine cavity altogether.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Peritoneal (abdominal) pregnancy is an ectopic implantation within the peritoneal cavity, not the normal uterine site.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: State that the normal implantation site is the posterior wall of the uterine body near the fundus.

questions.title: Implantation timing: the second week
questions.question: When does implantation occur?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The first week covers fertilisation and cleavage, from the zygote through to the free (unimplanted) blastocyst; implantation itself has not yet begun by its end.
explanations.B: Correct. Implantation is the defining event of the second week of development: it begins around day six or seven after fertilisation, when the blastocyst's embryonic pole adheres to the endometrium, and is essentially complete by around day eleven or twelve, once the surface epithelium has closed back over it. Every other landmark event of the second week — differentiation of the trophoblast into its two layers, formation of the amniotic cavity and primary yolk sac, and the appearance of extraembryonic mesoderm — follows directly on from this implantation process. This is why embryologists group the whole week around a single theme, sometimes summarised as "the week of twos": two trophoblast layers, two layers of the bilaminar disc, and two cavities forming around them.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third week is when gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar one; implantation is already complete well before this.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By the fourth week the embryo is folding and organs are beginning to form; implantation was completed two weeks earlier.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The fifth week belongs to the embryonic period of organogenesis, long after implantation is finished.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: State that implantation is the defining event of the second week of development.

questions.title: Outer trophoblast layer: syncytiotrophoblast
questions.question: What is the outer layer of the trophoblast?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytotrophoblast is the inner layer of the trophoblast, made of distinct mononuclear cells, not the outer invasive layer.
explanations.B: Correct. As the trophoblast differentiates during implantation, it splits into two layers: an inner cytotrophoblast of individual, mitotically active cells, and an outer syncytiotrophoblast in which the cell membranes between cells break down to form a single multinucleated mass. It is this outer syncytiotrophoblast that does the actual work of implantation, producing the proteolytic enzymes that erode the endometrial epithelium and stroma so the blastocyst can embed itself. Because the syncytiotrophoblast keeps proliferating outward from the cytotrophoblast beneath it, the inner layer is often described as the "germinal" layer that continually replenishes the invasive outer one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein coat around the oocyte and early embryo, already shed before implantation, not a layer of the trophoblast.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The corona radiata is the layer of granulosa cells surrounding the oocyte at ovulation, unrelated to the trophoblast layers of the later blastocyst.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The acrosome is a cap-like structure on the sperm head containing enzymes for fertilisation, not any part of the trophoblast.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Identify the syncytiotrophoblast as the outer, invasive layer of the trophoblast.

questions.title: Commonest site of tubal pregnancy: the ampulla
questions.question: What is the most common site for tubal pregnancy?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The narrow intramural part of the tube is a recognised but much less common site of tubal implantation than the ampulla.
explanations.B: Correct. A tubal (ectopic) pregnancy occurs when the blastocyst implants within the uterine tube instead of completing its journey to the uterine cavity, and the ampullary part of the tube, its widest and longest segment, is by far the commonest site for this to happen. This makes the uterine tube overall the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy of any kind, well ahead of the rarer ovarian, abdominal and cervical sites. The other named parts of the tube — the narrow intramural part passing through the uterine wall, and the fringed, funnel-shaped fimbriated end — are possible but much less frequent sites of tubal implantation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Implantation in the lower uterine segment describes placenta previa, an abnormal site within the uterus, not a tubal (ectopic) pregnancy at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fimbriated end of the tube is a possible site of tubal implantation, but it is far less common than the ampulla.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cervical pregnancy is a rare and distinct form of ectopic implantation, not a part of the uterine tube.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: State that the ampulla is the commonest site of tubal (ectopic) pregnancy.

questions.title: Placenta previa centralis
questions.question: Placenta previa centralis is best described as it………

options.C: Is away from the internal os
options.D: Is present in the posterior wall of the endometrium
options.E: Is present near the fundus of the uterus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Partial coverage of the os describes a lesser grade of placenta previa, not the "centralis" (complete) grade.
explanations.B: Correct. Placenta previa centralis (also called total or complete placenta previa) is the most severe grade of placenta previa, in which the placenta implants low in the uterus so that it completely covers the internal cervical os. Because the placenta lies directly across the entire opening the fetus must pass through, this grade carries the highest risk of major antepartum haemorrhage and makes vaginal delivery unsafe, so it is managed by caesarean section. It is the "centralis" (complete) end of a spectrum of low implantation, more severe than a placenta that only partially covers or merely approaches the os.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A placenta lying away from the internal os is not previa at all; placenta previa by definition involves the lower uterine segment near or over the os.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Implantation on the posterior wall near the fundus describes a normal implantation site, not the abnormal low, os-covering position of placenta previa centralis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A fundal placenta is a normal finding, essentially the opposite of a previa, which by definition lies low in the uterus near the internal os.

questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}

questions.title: What the decidua is
questions.question: What is the decidua?

explanations.A: Correct. The decidua is simply the name given to the functional layer of the endometrium once pregnancy has begun, so called because, like the rest of the functional layer in a non-pregnant cycle, it is shed at the end of pregnancy, at delivery. It is described in three named parts according to their relation to the developing conceptus — decidua basalis, decidua capsularis and decidua parietalis — each with its own fate as pregnancy progresses. Calling this tissue the "decidua" rather than simply "the endometrium" signals specifically that a conceptus has implanted and that this maternal tissue is now organised around it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The endometrium is called the decidua only once pregnancy has begun; before implantation it is simply the endometrium, going through its normal menstrual cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The myometrium is the muscular wall of the uterus, a completely different layer from the decidua, which is the modified endometrial (mucosal) lining.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This combines two wrong ideas: the decidua is endometrial, not muscular, tissue, and it exists only during pregnancy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The perimetrium is the thin outer serosal covering of the uterus, unrelated to the endometrial decidua.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Define the decidua as the endometrium of the pregnant uterus.

questions.title: Decidua basalis
questions.question: What is the decidua basalis?

options.A: The part between the blastula and the perimetrium
options.B: The part between the blastula and the endometrium
options.C: The part between the blastula and the myometrium
options.D: The part which covers the blastula
options.E: The part which lines the rest of the uterus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua basalis lies between the conceptus and the myometrium, not out as far as the thin outer perimetrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua basalis is itself a part of the endometrium (now called decidua), so it cannot lie "between" the conceptus and the endometrium.
explanations.C: Correct. Decidua basalis is the part of the decidua that lies deep to the implanted conceptus, sandwiched between it and the myometrium beneath, and it is this part specifically that goes on to form the maternal (decidual) plate of the placenta. Because it becomes a permanent, functioning component of the mature placenta, decidua basalis is the one part of the decidua's three named divisions that does not simply degenerate as pregnancy progresses. Its position deep to the conceptus, rather than covering it or lining the rest of the cavity, is exactly what earns it the name "basalis", from the same root as "base".
explanations.D: Incorrect. The decidual part that covers the conceptus is decidua capsularis, not decidua basalis, which lies underneath it instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lining the rest of the uterine cavity, away from the implantation site, describes decidua parietalis, not decidua basalis.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Name decidua basalis as the part of the decidua deep to the conceptus that becomes the maternal part of the placenta.

questions.title: Decidua capsularis
questions.question: What is the decidua capsularis?

options.A: The part between the blastula and the perimetrium
options.B: The part between the blastula and the endometrium
options.C: The part between the blastula and the myometrium
options.D: The part which covers the blastula
options.E: The part which lines the rest of the uterus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua capsularis covers the conceptus on the cavity side; it is not defined by any relation to the outer perimetrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua capsularis is itself part of the (now decidualised) endometrium, so it cannot lie between the conceptus and the endometrium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lying between the conceptus and the myometrium describes decidua basalis, not decidua capsularis, which instead covers the conceptus from the cavity side.
explanations.D: Correct. Decidua capsularis is the thin part of the decidua that stretches over the conceptus on the side facing the uterine cavity, effectively capping it off from the rest of the cavity. As the growing gestational sac expands over the following weeks, decidua capsularis is progressively stretched thinner and thinner until, by around the fourth month, it comes into contact with decidua parietalis on the opposite wall and the two fuse, obliterating the uterine cavity. Unlike decidua basalis, which persists as a functioning part of the mature placenta, decidua capsularis is eventually lost rather than incorporated into any permanent structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lining the rest of the uterine cavity away from the implantation site describes decidua parietalis, not decidua capsularis.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Name decidua capsularis as the part of the decidua that covers the conceptus and is later stretched and lost.

questions.title: Decidua parietalis
questions.question: What is the decidua parietalis?

options.A: The part between the blastula and the perimetrium
options.B: The part between the blastula and the endometrium
options.C: The part between the blastula and the myometrium
options.D: The part which covers the blastula
options.E: The part which lines the rest of the uterus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua parietalis is defined by its position lining the rest of the uterine cavity, not by any relation to the outer perimetrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua parietalis is itself decidualised endometrium; it does not sit "between" the conceptus and the endometrium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That description fits decidua basalis, which lies directly deep to the conceptus, not decidua parietalis, which lines the cavity elsewhere.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Covering the conceptus directly describes decidua capsularis, not decidua parietalis, which lines the rest of the cavity instead.
explanations.E: Correct. Decidua parietalis is the part of the decidua that lines the whole of the rest of the uterine cavity, everywhere away from the implantation site, and so away from both decidua basalis beneath the conceptus and decidua capsularis covering it. As the gestational sac enlarges, decidua capsularis is stretched against decidua parietalis on the opposite wall, and by about the fourth month the two fuse together, obliterating the uterine cavity as a distinct space. Decidua parietalis therefore does not become part of the placenta itself, unlike decidua basalis, but simply continues to line the uterus until it, together with the rest of the decidua, is shed at delivery.

questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Name decidua parietalis as the part of the decidua lining the rest of the uterine cavity.

questions.title: Placenta extending into the lower uterine segment
questions.question: Which one of the following conditions is mainly characterised by the placenta extending into the lower uterine segment?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A battledore placenta describes an abnormal, marginal insertion of the umbilical cord, not an abnormal position of the placenta itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A bipartate (bilobed) placenta is a shape abnormality, in which the placenta forms two separate lobes, unrelated to lower-segment implantation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A circumvallate placenta has an abnormal, rolled membrane insertion at its edge, again a structural rather than a positional abnormality.
explanations.D: Correct. Placenta previa is defined by exactly this feature: implantation of the placenta in the lower uterine segment, so that it lies near, partially over, or completely over the internal cervical os, instead of in its normal fundal or upper-wall position. Because it places placental tissue directly in the path the fetus must take at delivery, placenta previa is a well-recognised cause of antepartum haemorrhage and, in its more complete grades, requires delivery by caesarean section. This is a positional abnormality of the placenta, distinguished from other placental anomalies that instead involve its shape, its number of lobes, or its depth of invasion into the uterine wall.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A succenturiate placenta has one or more small accessory lobes separate from the main placental mass, a variation in number, not in the position of the main placenta.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Identify placenta previa as a positional abnormality involving the lower uterine segment.

questions.title: HCG source: the syncytiotrophoblast
questions.question: Which of the following cells secrete HCG to maintain pregnancy?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The embryoblast (inner cell mass) gives rise to the epiblast and hypoblast of the embryo proper; it does not itself secrete hormones into the maternal circulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The epiblast goes on to form all three germ layers of the embryo; hormone secretion into the mother's circulation is not part of its role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hypoblast contributes to the yolk sac lining, not to hormone secretion supporting the pregnancy.
explanations.D: Correct. Human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast, the outer, invasive layer of the trophoblast, from very early in implantation onward. HCG acts on the corpus luteum in the maternal ovary, signalling it to keep producing progesterone and so maintain the endometrium (decidua) of pregnancy instead of allowing it to break down as it would in a normal, non-pregnant cycle. Because it is produced this early and in rising amounts, and can be detected in maternal blood and urine, HCG is also the hormone that every standard pregnancy test is designed to detect.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cytotrophoblast is the inner, proliferative trophoblast layer that gives rise to the syncytiotrophoblast; it is the outer syncytial layer, not the cytotrophoblast itself, that does the secreting.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: State that the syncytiotrophoblast secretes HCG, which maintains the corpus luteum.

questions.title: Uterine layer where the placenta forms
questions.question: In which layer of the uterine wall is the placenta formed?

explanations.A: Correct. The placenta is formed by the union of a fetal part, the chorion frondosum, with a maternal part contributed by decidua basalis, the part of the decidua that lies directly deep to the implanted conceptus. Because decidua basalis persists throughout pregnancy as the maternal component of this exchange organ, it is the one part of the decidua that becomes a permanent, functioning structure rather than being stretched away or fused with another part and lost. The other two named parts of the decidua, capsularis and parietalis, instead thin out and eventually fuse with each other around the fourth month, taking no direct part in placental formation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua capsularis covers the conceptus on the cavity side and is progressively stretched and lost as pregnancy advances; it does not form the placenta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decidua parietalis simply lines the rest of the uterine cavity away from the implantation site and plays no part in forming the placenta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The myometrium is the muscular wall deep to the decidua; the placenta forms from the endometrial decidua basalis, not from uterine muscle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The perimetrium is the thin outer serosal covering of the uterus, far removed from the site of placental formation.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: State that the placenta forms from decidua basalis, together with the fetal chorion frondosum.

questions.title: The bilaminar germ disc forms the embryo proper
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the bilaminar germ disc is correct?

options.A: It consists of epiblast and mesoblast
options.B: It is derived from the outer cells of the morula
options.E: It appears at the middle of the first week

explanations.A: Incorrect. The bilaminar disc consists of epiblast and hypoblast, not mesoblast (mesoderm), which does not appear until gastrulation in the third week.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The bilaminar disc derives from the inner cell mass (embryoblast), not the outer cells of the morula, which instead give rise to the trophoblast.
explanations.C: Correct. The bilaminar embryonic disc, made up of the epiblast and the hypoblast, is what forms the embryo proper — it is from the epiblast layer of this disc that all three germ layers of the later trilaminar disc (ectoderm, intra-embryonic mesoderm and endoderm) arise the following week. Everything else derived from the blastocyst at this stage — the trophoblast layers, the yolk sac, the amnion — supports the pregnancy but does not itself become part of the fetus; only the bilaminar disc, and the structures the epiblast later produces from it, go on to build the embryo's own body. This is why the appearance of the bilaminar disc in the second week is considered the point at which the embryo proper is first laid down, even though it will not take on a recognisable three-layered structure until gastrulation in the third week.
explanations.D: Incorrect. HCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast, part of the trophoblast, not by the epiblast/hypoblast bilaminar disc.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The bilaminar disc appears around the eighth day, in the second week of development, not the first.

questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}

questions.title: Tissue of maternal origin: the decidua
questions.question: Which of the following tissues is of maternal origin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytotrophoblast is derived from the trophoblast of the blastocyst, and so is fetal, not maternal, in origin.
explanations.B: Correct. The decidua is maternal tissue: it is simply the mother's own endometrium, modified for pregnancy, and it is shed at delivery along with the fetal membranes. Every other structure listed instead derives from the conceptus itself — the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast are the two trophoblast layers that go on to form the fetal (chorionic) part of the placenta, while the amnion and yolk sac are extraembryonic membranes derived from the epiblast and hypoblast respectively. Distinguishing maternal decidua from these fetal-derived membranes matters clinically, because it is only the decidua basalis portion, together with the fetal chorion frondosum, that forms the definitive placenta at the maternal-fetal interface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Like the cytotrophoblast beneath it, the syncytiotrophoblast is trophoblast-derived and therefore fetal, not maternal, tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The amnion develops from the epiblast (via the amnioblast), making it a fetal, not a maternal, membrane.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The yolk sac is lined by hypoblast-derived cells, part of the conceptus, and so is fetal rather than maternal in origin.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Embryology > General Embryology > 2nd Week of Development
questions.source_citation: AEP Full Exams (VIP).pdf, Embryology Lecture (5) "2nd Week of Development", p.{page}
questions.learning_objective: Identify the decidua as maternal tissue, distinct from the fetal-derived trophoblast, amnion and yolk sac.

questions.title: Heuser's membrane lines the yolk sac
questions.question: Which of the following structures is lined by Heuser's (exocoelomic) membrane?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The blastocele is the cavity that Heuser's membrane lines and converts into the primary yolk sac; the membrane lines it, but the yolk sac is the structure it comes to define.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The amniotic cavity's roof is formed by the amnioblast, a trophoblast-facing cell population, not by Heuser's membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity) forms later, around day thirteen, from spaces opening up in the extraembryonic mesoderm, not from Heuser's membrane.
explanations.D: Correct. Heuser's membrane (also called the exocoelomic membrane) is a thin layer of flattened cells derived from the hypoblast, which spreads out to line the inside of the blastocele on about the ninth day, converting it into the primary yolk sac. This makes Heuser's membrane the original wall of the primary yolk sac, before that sac is later largely replaced by the smaller secondary (definitive) yolk sac, whose lining is laid down by a further wave of hypoblast-derived cells over Heuser's membrane. Its role is therefore purely structural at this early stage: it does not line the amniotic cavity, the extraembryonic coelom, or the decidua, each of which is a separate space or tissue formed by different cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The decidua is maternal endometrial tissue; Heuser's membrane is an embryonic structure derived from the hypoblast, with no connection to it.

questions.title: Adhesion and penetration into the endometrium: the trophoblast
questions.question: Which of the following structures is responsible for adhesion and penetration of the conceptus into the endometrium?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiblast is an inner-cell-mass derivative that goes on to form the embryo proper; it takes no part in eroding or adhering to the endometrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The embryoblast is the inner cell mass from which the epiblast and hypoblast arise; the outer trophoblast, not the embryoblast, does the work of implantation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The blastocele is simply the fluid-filled cavity within the blastocyst; it has no cells and cannot itself adhere to or penetrate anything.
explanations.D: Correct. It is the trophoblast, the outer cell layer of the blastocyst, that is responsible for both adhesion to and penetration into the endometrium during implantation. After the blastocyst's embryonic pole makes initial contact with the endometrial surface, the trophoblast there proliferates and differentiates into the outer syncytiotrophoblast, which produces the proteolytic enzymes that erode the endometrial epithelium and stroma, allowing the blastocyst to sink beneath the surface. The embryoblast, epiblast, hypoblast and blastocele, by contrast, are all inner structures of the blastocyst concerned with building the embryo itself, and play no direct part in the invasive process of implantation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The hypoblast lines the developing yolk sac and takes no part in adhesion to, or penetration of, the endometrium.
